content: Licorice, also spelled as liquorice, is derived from the root of the plant Glycyrrhiza glabra. This plant is a legume, closely related to beans and peas, and is native to southern Europe and parts of Asia. It is a herbaceous perennial that grows up to 1 meter in height, with pinnate leaves measuring approximately 7–15 centimeters in length, consisting of 9–17 leaflets. The plant produces flowers that are 1–2 centimeters long, ranging in color from purple to pale whitish-blue, arranged in loose inflorescences. Its fruit is an oblong pod, about 2–3 centimeters long, containing several seeds. Licorice is primarily cultivated as a root crop in southern Europe. Historically, it has been associated with Pontefract in Yorkshire, England, which hosts an annual licorice festival. In North America, commercial cultivation of licorice is minimal, and a related native species, American Licorice (Glycyrrhiza lepidota), is used instead. In northern China, Chinese Licorice (Glycyrrhiza uralensis) is cultivated for traditional Chinese medicine. Licorice thrives in deep, fertile, well-drained soils with full sun and is typically harvested in the autumn, two to three years after planting. Licorice extract is made by boiling the root and evaporating most of the water. The name licorice originates from the Ancient Greek words meaning sweet root. The extract is available in both solid and syrup forms, with its active compound, glycyrrhizin, being a sweetener over 50 times sweeter than sucrose and possessing pharmaceutical properties. Glycyrrhiza uralensis contains a higher concentration of glycyrrhizin. Licorice flavor is widely used in various candies, particularly in the United Kingdom, where licorice allsorts are popular. In continental Europe, stronger and saltier licorice candies are preferred. Many licorice-flavored candies, however, contain only small amounts of actual licorice, with the flavor often enhanced by aniseed oil. In the Netherlands, licorice candy, known as drop, is a popular treat, with some varieties mixed with mint, menthol, laurel, or ammonium chloride to create salty licorice. Licorice is also used in soft drinks like root beer and in herbal teas, providing a sweet aftertaste. It is commonly used in medicines to mask unpleasant flavors. In Italy, particularly in the south, licorice is consumed in its natural form, with the root simply dug up, washed, and chewed as a mouth freshener. Unsweetened licorice, made from 100% pure extract, is also popular in Italy, offering a bitter and intense taste. In Syria, licorice is sold as a drink, and dried licorice root can be chewed as a sweet. According to the USDA Food Database, black licorice contains approximately 100 calories per ounce (28 grams). In Chinese cuisine, licorice is used as a culinary spice for savory dishes, often flavoring broths and foods simmered in soy sauce. Similar flavors can be found in anise, star anise, tarragon, and fennel. Medicinally, powdered licorice root is an effective expectorant and has been used for this purpose since ancient times, particularly in Ayurvedic medicine, where it is also used in tooth powders. Modern cough syrups often include licorice extract. Licorice may also be beneficial in treating mouth ulcers and peptic ulcers. Non-prescription treatments for aphthous ulcers, such as Canker Melts, incorporate glycyrrhiza in dissolvable troches. Licorice is a mild laxative and can be used as a topical antiviral agent for conditions like shingles, ophthalmic herpes, oral herpes, and genital herpes. It influences the endocrine system due to its isoflavones (phytoestrogens), potentially lowering serum testosterone levels, though its effect on free testosterone remains unclear. High doses of glycyrrhizinic acid and glycyrrhetinic acid in licorice extract can lead to hypokalemia and significant increases in blood pressure, a condition known as apparent mineralocorticoid excess. This occurs due to the inhibition of the enzyme 11β-hydroxysteroid dehydrogenase type 2, which normally inactivates cortisol in the kidneys. As a result, cortisol levels appear elevated, mimicking the effects of aldosterone excess, even though aldosterone levels remain low or normal. To mitigate these side effects, deglycyrrhizinated licorice preparations are available. Licorice also inhibits Helicobacter pylori, aids in healing stomach and duodenal ulcers, and may soothe an upset stomach in moderate amounts. It can be used to treat ileitis, leaky gut syndrome, irritable bowel syndrome, and Crohn's disease due to its antispasmodic properties in the bowels. Licorice is an adaptogen that helps regulate the hypothalamic-pituitary-adrenal axis and may be used for autoimmune conditions such as lupus, scleroderma, rheumatoid arthritis, and animal dander allergies. In traditional Chinese medicine, licorice is commonly included in herbal formulas to harmonize the other ingredients, carry the formula into all 12 regular meridians, and relieve spasmodic coughs. It is also an important component in Fu Zheng anti-cancer formulas due to its anti-inflammatory properties. In traditional American herbalism, licorice is used in the Hoxsey anti-cancer formula. Excessive consumption of licorice or licorice candy can be toxic to the liver and cardiovascular system, potentially causing hypertension and edema. Rare cases of increased blood pressure have been reported with excessive consumption of licorice tea, but these effects are reversible upon discontinuation of the herb. Most cases of hypertension from licorice are attributed to overconsumption of concentrated licorice candy. Deglycyrrhizinated licorice is available to reduce the risk of these adverse effects.
